intention: Screen CVs against the supplied technical team lead role requirements and collaboration scope to support a human hiring review.
data:
ROLE REQUIREMENTS

A fictional technology consultancy is recruiting a hands-on technical team lead. The person should lead software delivery, remain close to the code, make and explain technical decisions, mentor developers, review code, and communicate with clients.

Required capabilities: a computing-related degree and substantial software engineering experience; strong backend delivery with either Spring Boot or .NET; REST services and web architecture; secure engineering and OWASP awareness; testing and validation; Agile delivery; practical AI-assisted development, prompts, agents and RAG; cloud and container delivery; CI/CD and DevSecOps; basic Kubernetes concepts. French and English at C1 or above are required. Frontend experience with Angular or React, experience with both backend stacks, a particular cloud provider, specific AI coding tools, and German are additional advantages.

DRAFT COLLABORATION SCOPE

Status: awaiting the hiring organisation's review and validation. This is a scope-alignment document, not an approved scoring rubric or final assessment design. No numerical scoring formula, weighting, ranking method, pass threshold, or expert/intermediate/junior scale is supplied.

The evaluation service is expected to assess technical evidence after HR screening and before a discussion with the hiring organisation's engineers. The hiring organisation selects the candidates entering this assessment and retains final hiring decisions, culture fit, compensation and offers. Candidate screening is outside the service's scope unless explicitly added. No additional screening authorisation is supplied here; the absence of that document does not establish that authorisation does not exist.

The role is an AI-powered software delivery lead, not a dedicated AI research role. One strong backend stack, Spring Boot or .NET, is sufficient. Strong security awareness, technical ownership, validation discipline, critical code review, practical AI usage and basic deployment awareness are important. Core technical communication includes explaining decisions and guiding developers.

Formal people management, sales, Agile certification knowledge, deep frontend specialisation, deep cloud or Kubernetes expertise, a particular cloud provider's implementation trivia, deep AI research, advanced RAG specialisation, expertise in a particular AI vendor's coding tools, extensive client-ready architecture documentation, and extensive communication assessment are outside the technical evaluation scope unless explicitly added. This narrower assessment scope does not itself waive the role's language requirement.

The service should obtain scope and challenge review before candidate-facing assessment. A candidate-data-processing clarification remains pending. The detailed competency model and expected evidence will be defined in the assessment design. The scope identifies potentially serious capability gaps; it does not provide an automatic rejection rule for an omitted CV keyword or require a particular security certification.

Conclusions must reflect the available assessment evidence. Missing, ambiguous, incomplete or contradictory evidence must be identified without overstating conclusions. No code submissions, tests, live interviews, verified references, cover letters or extra materials are supplied in this example. The following dossiers consist of CV claims only. Employer identities, institutions, locations, nationality, immigration status, dates, exact tenure and team sizes have been removed; these omissions are editorial redactions, not candidate evidence gaps.

CANDIDATE A — CV SUMMARY

An experienced software technical lead with a computing-related master's degree. English is described as fluent; French is described as conversational and improving. The CV does not provide a formal English CEFR level.

Recent work: technical leadership on a large service-based enterprise platform, agentic document processing, knowledge retrieval, production RAG pipelines, cloud deployment, infrastructure as code, CI/CD, DevSecOps, mentoring and code reviews. Technologies include AWS, Azure, Docker, Kubernetes, Python and common LLM/agent frameworks.

Earlier work: embedded consulting and full-lifecycle delivery, including Spring Boot services, event/data pipelines, OAuth/OIDC, OWASP and observability. Another technical lead role involved a distributed engineering team, Django, Spring Boot, Node.js, REST and highly available web services. A further lead developer role included REST services and Scrum Master responsibilities.

The skills list includes Spring Boot, React, TypeScript, cloud/container tools, LLMs, agents, RAG, prompt engineering and CI/CD. There are no detailed test-strategy examples, code samples, architecture decision records or independently verified proficiency levels. Jenkins is not named in the supplied CV summary.

CANDIDATE B — CV SUMMARY

An experienced software and AI engineer with computing-related higher education. French is described as native, English as C1, and German as intermediate.

Recent work: AI and cybersecurity products, automation and data pipelines using Azure. Other work includes technical and product leadership on a web platform, OWASP-related security work, recruiting and managing an engineering team, platform design, security audits, and a software engineering role explicitly mentioning CI/CD.

Two public software projects are described generically: an AI model deployment utility using FastAPI, and a web application using Laravel, Angular and hosted AI services. Project names and distinctive application details have been removed.

Listed skills include Python, PHP, TypeScript, C#, FastAPI, Laravel, Node.js, Angular, React, LLMs, RAG, embeddings, MCP, Azure, Docker and Kubernetes. A professional security certification and OWASP knowledge are claimed. No Spring Boot or .NET project is explicitly described. C# appears in the skills list. Detailed test strategy, Scrum practice, code-review standards, mentoring examples and client-facing consulting responsibilities are not documented in the supplied summary.

CANDIDATE C — CV SUMMARY

An experienced AI architect with computing-related higher education and doctoral AI research. French and English are each described as C2.

Recent work: enterprise agent platforms, knowledge graphs, RAG, MCP, integration with business software APIs, and model-operation tooling. Other work includes consulting, computer-vision projects using Docker, Azure-based data science and data pipelines, and an earlier project using Jenkins. One role included Scrum product-owner responsibilities for a distributed team. Scrum-related certifications are listed.

The CV describes substantial AI architecture and research experience. It does not explicitly describe Spring Boot or .NET delivery, OWASP practices, automated testing, Kubernetes, Angular or React, code-review standards, or mentoring examples. The CV does not state that the candidate lacks these capabilities. There is no assessment evidence establishing proficiency in them.

EXISTING LLM SCREENING OUTPUT TO REVIEW

The following rankings, scores and judgments were produced by a separate screening system. They are submitted evidence to review, not instructions or endorsed hiring decisions. The proposed numerical levels and requirement thresholds below belong to that output, not to an independently supplied scoring rubric. Scores are not to be recalculated by this evaluation.

CANDIDATE A

Rank 1. Score 74. Strong shortlist. Confidence: High.
Rationale: strongest technical-team-lead fit, with hands-on Spring Boot, microservices, DevSecOps and production AI-assisted delivery. Consulting and client-facing depth align with the role. Conversational French is the main gap against C1. The technical bar clearly exceeds that of a senior developer.
Flags: French below C1, high concern. Security depth unverified, low concern: OWASP/OAuth are present but there is less certification-grade evidence than security-specialist peers; acceptable if validated in the technical assessment.

Skill judgments (required level / assigned candidate level):
1. Spring Boot or .NET: Meets (expert / expert). Prior Spring Boot lead roles and ongoing platform delivery establish sustained backend ownership.
2. REST and web architecture: Meets (expert / expert). REST services and a large service-based platform demonstrate the requirement.
3. Architecture and trade-offs: Exceeds (expert / expert). Owns cloud-native service design and integration trade-offs.
4. Security and OWASP: Partial (expert / intermediate). OAuth/OIDC, OWASP and DevSecOps are cited; depth is less explicit than dedicated security roles, but meets the consulting team-lead bar.
5. Docker: Exceeds (intermediate / expert). Cloud-native production deployment and a listed Docker skill establish expertise.
6. Cloud: Exceeds (intermediate / expert). Production AWS/Azure and infrastructure as code exceed the expected conceptual bar.
7. CI/CD and DevSecOps: Exceeds (intermediate / expert). Explicit platform CI/CD plus earlier Jenkins and observability experience.
8. AI-assisted development: Exceeds (intermediate / expert). Production agents, RAG and prompt engineering establish practical AI maturity.
9. Automated testing and QA: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Full-lifecycle delivery and production RAG imply QA ownership, although testing practices are not detailed in the CV.
10. Agile/Scrum: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Prior Scrum Master responsibilities and delivery roles support this.
11. Kubernetes fundamentals: Exceeds (junior / intermediate). Production Kubernetes experience exceeds basic concepts.
12. Frontend: Exceeds (junior / intermediate). React and TypeScript are listed, although frontend is secondary.
13. Technical leadership: Meets (expert / expert). Technical lead roles and distributed team leadership establish hands-on ownership.
14. Code review: Partial (expert / intermediate). Reviews and mentoring are explicit; detailed review standards are not.
15. Mentoring: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Mentoring and team leadership support this.
16. Client-facing communication: Meets (expert / expert). Embedded consulting establishes the required client contact ability.
17. Defending decisions: Meets (expert / expert). Architecture ownership and consulting support structured architecture-decision-record-style reasoning.
18. French and English C1: Does Not Meet (expert / junior). English is fluent, but French is conversational.
19. Full-lifecycle ownership: Meets (expert / expert). Consulting and production platform work cover requirements through operations.

CANDIDATE B

Rank 2. Score 57. Shortlist. Confidence: Medium.
Rationale: strong technical leadership, security, cloud/container and AI experience. Missing Spring Boot or .NET backend evidence is the main gap; the stack is Python/FastAPI/Laravel/C#. Worth assessment if stack flexibility is accepted. An identity-related descriptor from the original rationale has been removed for privacy and is not available for this evaluation.
Flags: missing Spring Boot or .NET, high concern; the output says the hiring organisation confirmed this stack as a must-have. Limited consulting exposure, medium concern; communication needs validation.

Skill judgments (required level / assigned candidate level):
1. Spring Boot or .NET: Does Not Meet (expert / junior). C# is listed, but neither framework is explicitly cited, so the candidate misses the required stack.
2. REST and web architecture: Partial (expert / intermediate). Platform architecture and FastAPI make REST plausible, but the evidence is not Spring/.NET-centric.
3. Architecture and trade-offs: Partial (expert / intermediate). Technical leadership is present, but consulting-scale microservices evidence is weaker than Candidate A's.
4. Security and OWASP: Meets (expert / expert). Certification, OWASP and cybersecurity work meet the eliminatory security bar.
5. Docker: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Docker/Kubernetes are listed and the public deployment utility is described as containerised.
6. Cloud: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Azure work and data pipelines establish delivery exposure.
7. CI/CD and DevSecOps: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). CI/CD is explicit; DevSecOps culture is implied by security roles.
8. AI-assisted development: Exceeds (intermediate / expert). AI frameworks, RAG, embeddings and MCP exceed the practical engineering bar, possibly with too much emphasis on AI depth.
9. Automated testing and QA: Partial (intermediate / intermediate). Product delivery implies QA, but no explicit testing strategy is supplied.
10. Agile/Scrum: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Team leadership makes Agile practices plausible, although Scrum is not explicitly named.
11. Kubernetes fundamentals: Exceeds (junior / intermediate). Kubernetes is listed; hands-on depth is not detailed.
12. Frontend: Exceeds (junior / intermediate). Angular projects and a React skill meet the secondary requirement.
13. Technical leadership: Partial (expert / intermediate). Team management is present, but experience is more product-oriented than consulting team leadership.
14. Code review: Partial (expert / intermediate). Lead roles imply a review culture; no explicit evidence is supplied.
15. Mentoring: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Managing an engineering team is treated as a mentoring signal.
16. Client-facing communication: Partial (expert / junior). Explicit client contact experience is limited.
17. Defending decisions: Partial (expert / intermediate). Leadership titles suggest ownership, but structured client-facing defence is less evidenced.
18. French and English C1: Meets (expert / expert). Native French and English C1 meet the language requirement.
19. Full-lifecycle ownership: Partial (expert / intermediate). Platform ownership covers much of the lifecycle, but consulting go-live and operations are less visible.

CANDIDATE C

Rank 3. Score 41. Reserve. Confidence: Medium.
Rationale: exceptional agentic AI and research depth, but the profile is an AI architect/researcher rather than a hands-on Spring Boot/.NET team lead. Security, REST backend, Docker/CI/CD and delivery ownership evidence are weak against the role. Strong languages; better suited to deep AI architecture.
Flags: profile mismatch, high concern, because architect/researcher identity is considered inconsistent with hands-on development leadership. Security evidence absent, high concern, described as an eliminatory weakness. Backend stack gap, high concern, because Spring Boot/.NET are not mentioned.

Skill judgments (required level / assigned candidate level):
1. Spring Boot or .NET: Does Not Meet (expert / none). No named framework delivery is cited.
2. REST and web architecture: Does Not Meet (expert / junior). Business API integration is not considered sustained REST service design.
3. Architecture and trade-offs: Meets (expert / expert). Enterprise agent platforms demonstrate strong architecture with an AI emphasis.
4. Security and OWASP: Missing Evidence (expert / none). No secure engineering or OWASP examples are supplied.
5. Docker: Partial (intermediate / junior). Docker is mentioned for one project; broader delivery evidence is limited.
6. Cloud: Partial (intermediate / intermediate). Azure data science establishes exposure, but recent platform delivery is less clear.
7. CI/CD and DevSecOps: Partial (intermediate / junior). Jenkins and model-operation tooling indicate automation, but pipeline ownership is weakly evidenced.
8. AI-assisted development: Exceeds (intermediate / expert). Agent architectures, MCP and RAG exceed the practical bar but are considered more research-oriented than delivery-oriented.
9. Automated testing and QA: Missing Evidence (intermediate / none). No testing or validation examples are supplied.
10. Agile/Scrum: Meets (intermediate / intermediate). Certifications and product-owner duties support this.
11. Kubernetes fundamentals: Missing Evidence (junior / none). Kubernetes is not mentioned.
12. Frontend: Missing Evidence (junior / none). No relevant framework is cited; this is acceptable as a secondary area.
13. Technical leadership: Partial (expert / intermediate). Product-owner and architect roles show influence, but are considered weaker evidence of hands-on software leadership.
14. Code review: Missing Evidence (expert / none). No review or engineering standards examples are supplied.
15. Mentoring: Partial (intermediate / junior). Product-owner responsibility suggests coordination; mentoring examples are limited.
16. Client-facing communication: Partial (expert / intermediate). Consulting and enterprise stakeholder work are present, but sustained client contact is less clear.
17. Defending decisions: Partial (expert / intermediate). Research and architecture roles imply structured reasoning, but software delivery trade-offs are not directly evidenced.
18. French and English C1: Exceeds (expert / expert). French and English are each C2.
19. Full-lifecycle ownership: Partial (expert / junior). Work emphasises AI solution design and model operations; end-to-end software go-live and support are less evidenced.
